report:
**Conclusion: yes—offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) in addition to usual testing options generally causes more people to test.** The strongest evidence comes from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), synthesized in systematic reviews, rather than from simple before-and-after comparisons.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs in the general population found that HIVST increased testing uptake across multiple delivery approaches (for example, direct distribution and partner distribution). It also found that HIVST could identify people who might otherwise not test, with positivity and linkage outcomes broadly comparable with standard services.  
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext

The evidence is especially consistent among key populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender people: a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs concluded that free HIVST-kit distribution increased testing uptake versus standard care in every subgroup analysis. It found no evidence of substantial social harms or worse condom use.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z

Individual RCT evidence supports a causal interpretation. In Seattle, providing self-tests to MSM at high risk increased the frequency of HIV testing compared with standard care.  
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6037557/

**Important caveat:** more testing is not automatically the same as better outcomes. A large UK trial found regular free kits increased testing frequency, but did not demonstrate faster HIV diagnosis or linkage to care. Programs should therefore pair self-tests with clear instructions for confirmatory testing and rapid access to treatment/prevention services.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11801452/
